Chapter 6: Confidence in Action—Turning Thought into Practice
Have you ever noticed that real confidence doesn’t just appear out of thin air? It’s not something you simply think yourself into—it’s something you build, step by step, by actually doing. Today, let’s dig into the practical side of confidence: how you can move from just wanting to feel more self-assured, to actually showing up in the world with that confidence. Here’s the big idea: confidence grows through action, not just intention. Sure, reflecting and shifting your mindset is helpful, but it’s only when you put things into practice that you really start to see a change. Think about learning to swim. You can read every book and watch every video about swimming, but until you get in the water and start moving your arms, you won’t really learn how to swim—or feel confident doing it. So, how do you actually make this leap from thought to action? It helps to use what I like to call the “action loop.”
First, act—even before you feel ready. Don’t wait for the perfect moment or for a surge of confidence to magically show up. Take a small step forward. It might feel uncomfortable at first, but the very act of doing something new starts to build those feelings of capability. It’s like lighting a match: the spark comes from action itself. Next, learn from whatever happens. Maybe things go well, maybe they don’t. Either way, you get feedback. Every experience, win or lose, teaches you something and adds to your sense of “Hey, I can handle this.” Then, repeat and expand. With each cycle, your comfort zone stretches just a little bit more. What once felt intimidating starts to feel routine, and you realize you’re capable of more than you thought. Let’s look at a simple example. Imagine someone who finds it tough to speak up in meetings. Instead of waiting until they feel totally confident, they decide to make just one short comment per meeting. It could be as simple as agreeing with someone else or asking a clarifying question. Over time, that single step gets easier—and before long, they’re sharing ideas and maybe even leading parts of the discussion.
To make this process easier, try breaking big goals into micro-actions. Ask yourself, “What’s the smallest thing I can do today that moves me forward?” Tiny steps count, and they add up. Also, keep track of your progress. Even a simple checklist or quick notes in your phone can help you see how far you’ve come. And don’t forget to reward effort—not just the outcome. Celebrate the fact that you tried, regardless of how it turned out. That little bit of recognition goes a long way toward building real, lasting confidence. This approach is especially powerful if you tend to doubt yourself or worry about making mistakes. When you focus on taking action instead of being perfect, it’s easier to get out of your head and start building confidence through actual experience. Supportive environments make a huge difference, too. Teams and organizations that encourage people to try new things, accept mistakes as part of the process, and recognize effort—not just results—create a culture where confidence can really take root. If you’re a leader, you can help by sharing your own learning journey and giving others the space to take risks.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? Confidence isn’t a finish line you cross. It’s a daily practice—a series of choices to step forward, learn, and grow. The more you do, the more confident you become. And that’s something worth building, one action at a time.
